title: Organizing: is this approach effective, and why?
blurb: Judge board composition, role combinations, assurance independence, delegated change authority and the organizational design and development technique in a scenario.
question: To save money, Wenmoor Community Health proposes that its director of operations acts as both executive and project manager for the single point of access project. Is this appropriate, and why?

teach.h: A structure that can actually direct, manage and deliver
teach.body: Formally, the organizing practice defines and establishes the project's structure of accountability and responsibilities. In plain English: one person clearly accountable, the business, user and supplier interests all represented on the board, assurance that does not depend on the project manager, and a team designed around the real organization. BL4 items describe a structure or a change to it and ask whether it is effective; the answer usually rests on a role rule or a step of the organizational design and development technique.

head: Proposal
Verdict
Rule
rows: Executive cannot be combined with PM
teach.caption: Executive accountability cannot be delegated. Senior user and senior supplier may each be more than one person (6.2.4).

teach.h: Assurance: independent of the PM, not of the project
teach.body: Board members are accountable for assurance of their own area (business, user, supplier), even if they delegate the work to someone in the business or an external party. The board decides how assurance is done. Project assurance cannot be delegated to the project manager, project team members or project support, and project support must be kept separate from assurance so that its independence is protected.

teach.caption: The five steps of the technique (6.3.1), shaped by the WBS and the commercial management approach.

teach.body: The project board is the ultimate authority for requests for change and off-specifications, but it may delegate approval to a change authority or to the project manager, within limits and normally with a change budget so approved changes can be funded. The delegation is documented in the issue management approach and the relevant role descriptions, and reviewed at each stage boundary or when tolerances change. Delegation covers approving changes, not implementing them.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Wenmoor's single point of access
teach.body: Karen Lindqvist, director of operations and budget holder, becomes executive. Moira Healy, head of nursing for Eastfield, who will lead the triage hub, is a senior user. Tim Rawlings of Medivault and Josie Barker, the clinical systems manager, are senior suppliers. Neil Ashworth's internal audit and assurance team, independent of operational services and of project manager Ellie Chandran, provides assurance. The board delegates minor form and rota changes to a change authority with a small change budget.

rows.label: Purpose
values: Confirm the project is run right

teach.text: Classic traps: the executive and project manager roles are never combined, however small the budget; and assurance done by the PM, a project team member or project support is not assurance. The project management team structure has no authority of its own: the board directs within the remit set by the business layer.

items: Identify what is proposed: a board member, a combined role, an assurance choice, a delegation or a technique step.
Test it against the role rules: one executive, not the PM; assurance independent of the PM.
Check the three interests are all represented and roles reflect capability, authority and availability.
Decide the verdict, then choose the reason that explains it, not a true but unrelated fact.
One executive, never combined with the PM; accountability cannot be delegated (6.2.4.1).
PM may also be team manager and project support, depending on skill and capacity (6.2.4.5).
Assurance cannot be the PM, project team members or project support (6.2.4.7).
Change authority: delegated by the board within limits, with a change budget, reviewed at stage boundaries (10.2.4).
Technique: understand, design, develop, manage changes, transition (6.3.1).

summary: You can now judge whether a project's board, role combinations, assurance and change authority are set up effectively. You can also recognize each step of the organizational design and development technique in a scenario.

A.q: Wenmoor Community Health is starting up its single point of access project. Project manager Ellie Chandran runs workshops to map how decisions are made in the trust, which approvals need the trust board, how clinical staff are managed across the three localities and the rules for consulting the nursing union. Which step of the organizational design and development technique is she applying?
options: Design the project ecosystem
Develop the project ecosystem
Manage ongoing changes to the project ecosystem
Understand the organizational ecosystem
A.why: Understanding the organizational ecosystem means learning its existing structures, governance, decisions needing business approval, people management and policies (6.3.1).

whyNot.0: Designing the project ecosystem decides how to organize the project's own work and people, after the existing organization is understood.
whyNot.1: Developing the project ecosystem covers onboarding, skills and culture once the project team exists.
whyNot.2: Managing ongoing changes adjusts the project ecosystem as needs change during the lifecycle.

A.q: Wenmoor Community Health's trust executive team commissions the single point of access project. Karen Lindqvist is to be executive and Ellie Chandran project manager. Which role should be accountable for these two appointments?
options: The business layer
The executive
The project board
The senior user
A.why: In 'appoint the executive and the project manager' the business layer is accountable and the executive responsible (13.4.1).

whyNot.1: The executive is responsible for the activity; accountability sits with the business layer.
whyNot.2: The project board is not yet formed when the executive and PM are appointed.
whyNot.3: The senior user is appointed later, as part of the project management team.

A.q: Wenmoor Community Health needs a senior user for its single point of access pilot in Eastfield. Candidates are: Moira Healy, head of nursing for Eastfield, who will lead the triage hub; Tim Rawlings, the patient record supplier's account manager; Neil Ashworth, head of internal audit and assurance; and Ellie Chandran, the project manager. Who is most appropriate?
options: Tim Rawlings
Neil Ashworth
Moira Healy
Ellie Chandran
A.why: The senior user represents those who will use the products and specifies the benefits; Moira leads the nurses who will run and use the triage hub (6.2.4.2).

whyNot.0: Tim represents the supplier, so he fits senior supplier.
whyNot.1: Neil runs an independent assurance function, which suits project assurance.
whyNot.3: Ellie manages the project day to day for the board; she does not represent the nurses who will use the hub.

B.q: On Wenmoor's single point of access project, project manager Ellie Chandran offers to provide user assurance to the board herself, because she was seconded from the quality team and is trained in quality improvement methods. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Accept, because her quality background suits an assurance role
Ask project support to give user assurance in her place
Appoint someone independent of the PM to give assurance
Ask the team managers to assure each other's products
B.why: Project assurance must be independent of the project manager; it cannot be done by the PM, project team members or project support (6.2.4.7).

whyNot.0: Her skills do not change the rule: the PM cannot perform project assurance.
whyNot.1: Project support must be kept separate from project assurance.
whyNot.3: Team managers checking each other's products is quality control within delivery; it does not give the board independent assurance on behalf of the users.

B.q: Wenmoor's single point of access is in its final stage. Ellie Chandran arranges for the triage hub, its rotas, its staff and the lessons learned to pass to the operational managers who will run the service once the project closes. Which step of the organizational design and development technique is this?
options: Manage ongoing changes to the project ecosystem
Transition into the organizational ecosystem
Develop the project ecosystem
Design the project ecosystem
B.why: The final step transitions the project into the organizational ecosystem: products, people and learning are handed back to the business at closure (6.3.1).

whyNot.0: Managing ongoing changes adjusts the project team during the lifecycle, not the final handback.
whyNot.2: Developing the project ecosystem covers onboarding, skills and culture during the project.
whyNot.3: Designing decides how the project's work and people will be organized at the start.

B.q: Wenmoor's single point of access is in the 'starting up a project' process. Karen Lindqvist, the executive, asks project manager Ellie Chandran to choose and appoint the senior supplier. Which statement about responsibility for this appointment is correct?
options: The project manager is responsible, with the executive accountable
The executive is responsible, with the business layer accountable
The senior user is responsible, with the board accountable
The project board is responsible, with the PM consulted
B.why: In 'appoint the project management team' the executive is responsible and the business layer accountable; the PM is not involved (13.4.4).

whyNot.0: The project manager is not involved in appointing the project management team.
whyNot.2: The senior user is one of the roles being appointed, not the person appointing.
whyNot.3: The board is formed by this activity; the PM is not involved in it.

C.q: Wenmoor Community Health is starting up its single point of access project with a budget of £650,000. To keep costs down, the trust's executive team proposes that Karen Lindqvist, director of operations and budget holder, acts as both executive and project manager. Is this an appropriate application of the 'organizing' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because she holds the budget and can secure the funding
Yes, because the PM may also perform team manager and support roles
No, because the executive role cannot be combined with the PM
No, because the executive must be appointed by the commissioner
C.why: There can be only one executive, and the role cannot be combined with the project manager role (6.2.4.1).

whyNot.0: Holding the budget makes Karen a good executive, but it does not allow her to be the PM as well.
whyNot.1: It is true the PM may also be team manager and support, but that says nothing about combining with the executive.
whyNot.3: The business layer, here the trust's executive team, identifies the executive.

C.q: On Wenmoor's single point of access project, the board asks the project support officer, who maintains the registers for Ellie Chandran, to also provide user assurance on the Eastfield pilot because she knows the project's records well. Is this an appropriate application of the 'organizing' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because board members can delegate their assurance work
Yes, because the board decides how project assurance is carried out
No, because user assurance must be given by the senior user in person
No, because project support must be kept separate from assurance
C.why: Project support must be kept separate from project assurance to maintain the independence of assurance (6.2.4.7).

whyNot.0: Board members can delegate assurance, but not to project support.
whyNot.1: The board decides how assurance is done, but within the rule that support and assurance stay separate.
whyNot.2: Board members may delegate assurance work to others; they keep the accountability.

C.q: Wenmoor's single point of access is about to start its design stage. Project manager Ellie Chandran is new to PRINCE2 7, and several clinicians on the team have never worked on a project. Ellie arranges coaching for herself and short induction sessions for team members before the work starts. How well does this apply the 'organizing' practice, and why?
options: Well, because developing the ecosystem includes onboarding and skills
Well, because the project manager role should not be shared
Poorly, because training is a business matter outside the project
Poorly, because the senior user is accountable for team skills
C.why: Developing the project ecosystem includes onboarding and skills assessment, and building effective teams means closing capability gaps, for example by upskilling (6.3.1, 3.3.2).

whyNot.1: It is true the PM role should not be shared, but that does not explain why coaching and induction are good practice.
whyNot.2: Closing competency gaps is part of developing the project ecosystem, not something left outside the project.
whyNot.3: The senior user represents users; the team's capability is addressed through the project's own development of its ecosystem.

reteach.title: Four rules that settle most organizing questions
reteach.question: Which four role rules let you judge most proposed project structures in seconds?

blocks.body: One: there is exactly one executive, and that person is never the project manager. Two: the PM may also be team manager and project support if skill and capacity allow. Three: assurance is independent of the PM, so never the PM, a project team member or project support. Four: the board may delegate change approval within limits, with a change budget, recorded in the issue management approach and role descriptions.

blocks.text: An option can quote a true rule and still be the wrong reason. 'The PM may also be team manager' is true, but it does not justify making the PM the executive.

explain.body: There is one executive, the single point of accountability, whose accountability cannot be delegated and whose role cannot be combined with the PM. The PM role should not be shared, but the PM may also act as team manager and project support.

test.q: On Wenmoor's single point of access project, the board suggests that Karen Lindqvist and the commissioning manager share the executive role, because both care about the contract. What is the main problem?
options: The PM must approve shared roles
Two senior users would be needed
There can be only one executive
Executives must come from suppliers
test.why: There cannot be more than one executive; it is the single point of accountability (6.2.4.1).

whyNot.0: The PM does not approve board roles.
whyNot.1: The number of senior users is not the issue.
whyNot.3: Executives represent the business interest, not suppliers.

explain.body: Project assurance is the board's responsibility, independent of the PM but not of the project. It can be done by board members, people from the business or external parties.

test.q: Wenmoor's board wants business assurance independent of the project manager. Neil Ashworth's internal audit and assurance team is independent of operational services. Is it suitable?
options: Yes, it can also take on the project support role
Yes, it is independent of the project manager
No, assurance must be external to the trust
No, internal audit reports to the audit committee instead
test.why: Assurance can be appointed from within the business as long as it is independent of the PM (6.2.4.7).

whyNot.0: Support must stay separate from assurance.
whyNot.2: Assurance may come from the business or from outside.
whyNot.3: Its reporting line does not stop it giving assurance to the board.

explain.body: The board may delegate approval of requests for change and off-specifications to a change authority or the PM, within limits and with a change budget, documented in the issue management approach and role descriptions, and reviewed at stage boundaries.

test.q: Wenmoor's board delegates to Moira Healy and Josie Barker the approval of small changes to referral forms, up to £8,000 in total. Where should this delegation be documented?
options: The issue management approach and their role descriptions
The quality management approach and their role descriptions
The communication management approach
The daily log and the next highlight report
test.why: Delegated change authority is documented in the issue management approach and the relevant role descriptions (10.2.4).

whyNot.1: The quality management approach covers quality techniques, standards and responsibilities, not change authority.
whyNot.2: The communication approach covers communication with stakeholders.
whyNot.3: The daily log and highlight report do not set standing authority.

explain.body: Understand the organizational ecosystem; design the project ecosystem; develop it (onboarding, skills, culture); manage ongoing changes to it; transition the project back into the organizational ecosystem.

items.label: Design teams and ways of working

test.q: Because most Wenmoor team members work part-time on rotas and can only meet online at lunchtime, Ellie Chandran decides how work, people and meetings will be organized for the project. Which step is this?
options: Understand the organizational ecosystem
Transition into the organizational ecosystem
Manage ongoing changes to the project ecosystem
Design the project ecosystem
test.why: Designing the project ecosystem decides how to organize the work and people, including integrated ways of working (6.3.1).

whyNot.0: Understanding maps the existing organization, which comes first.
whyNot.2: Managing ongoing changes adjusts the design later in the lifecycle.
